Reproducing Xia et al. (2021) from SPARC:108 and SPARC:75¶

Paper. Xia J, Yang H, Mu M, Micovic N, Poskanzer KE, Monaghan JR, Clark HA (2021). Imaging in vivo acetylcholine release in the peripheral nervous system with a fluorescent nanosensor. PNAS 118:e2023807118. doi:10.1073/pnas.2023807118. The claims file (claims/xia-2021.yaml) was written from the version of record and its SI Appendix (Figures S1 to S16, Table S1); Movies S1 to S4 were not available.

Datasets. Both are read anonymously from the public SPARC bucket at a pinned published version, through the version's manifest.json and each file's S3 object version (xia2021.py). The cell after the imports lists every file read, with its SHA-256 from the manifest.

  • SPARC:108, version 1 (doi:10.26275/w027-cisv), "Imaging in vivo acetylcholine release in the peripheral nervous system with a fluorescent nanosensor in mice": HPLC chromatograms, UV-Vis spectra and native PAGE images; ex vivo calibration recordings (sub-1); in vivo recordings at 3 V (sub-2), 8 V (sub-3) and 10 V (sub-4); a confocal stack of a nanosensor-stained ChAT(BAC)-eGFP ganglion (sub-5); and the vesamicol pair (sub-6).
  • SPARC:75, version 1 (doi:10.26275/prjd-jhoc), "Submandibular ganglion stained by bungarotoxin and nanosensors developed by the Clark lab": confocal LSM images of one ChAT(BAC)-eGFP ganglion stained with BTX-AF647 or the nanosensor.

Why these versions. The paper's Data Availability cites the DOI of version 1 of SPARC:108 (10.26275/w027-cisv), so that version is pinned. The paper cites no version of SPARC:75; version 1 is its only published version (Pennsieve Discover lists one version of each dataset), so it is pinned. No version comparison is needed.

Claims. 29 claims; 12 are analysed here, 11 of them with an outcome and figs12-3v-propagation blocked as the deposit holds one of its three mice, and 18 blocked in all.

fig4b-lod tested (one mouse of three)

fig5b-control-minimal blocked: no control nanosensor recordings (data_missing)
figs8-control-10v blocked: no control nanosensor recordings (data_missing)
fig5c-voltage-dose blocked: no 5 V recording, and 3 V and 10 V come from different mice (data_missing)
fig5c-ach-concentration blocked: depends on fig5c-voltage-dose and figs6b-unit-calibration
fig5d-pulse-dose blocked: no recordings with 10 or 50 pulses (data_missing)
fig5e-reversibility blocked: no recording with three repeated stimulations (data_missing)
figs7b-in-vitro-reversibility blocked: no dialysis-fiber recording (data_missing)
fig6-vesamicol tested (one experiment of four)
figs9-aqua-vs-roi blocked: AQuA (MATLAB) cannot run in this environment (not_runnable)
figs10-control-8v blocked: no control nanosensor recordings (data_missing)
fig7-rostral-caudal tested (sub-3; block onsets in place of AQuA, which cannot run here)
fig7-peak-timing tested (sub-3; block onsets in place of AQuA)
figs12-3v-propagation blocked: one mouse of three deposited (data_missing); analysed on sub-2 and sub-3, that one mouse, with block onsets in place of AQuA
figs16-af647-stable tested
figs13-two-photon blocked: no two-photon images (data_missing)

Method details the claims file leaves open are taken from the paper where it gives them, and every reading the claims file names is run; each choice is cited in xia2021.py and in the section that uses it.

# Every file this notebook reads, with its size and SHA-256 from the pinned version's manifest (the header's
# checksums; the last cell checks that nothing else was read).
def files_read():
    out = {"108": ["files/dataset_description.xlsx", "files/subjects.xlsx", "files/primary/manifest.xlsx"]
                  + [X.SC + f"HPLC_{c}.csv" for c in ("PHAB", "260_NM", "280_NM", "652_NM")]
                  + [X.SC + n for n in ("2019-08-09_sensor.xml", "2019-08-09_dna_scaffold.xml")]
                  + [X.SC + f"2019-08-09_SENSOR_{c}.tif" for c in ("eb", "PHAB", "AF652")]
                  + list(X.MOVIES.values()) + [X.CZI_SUB5, X.SV + "sub-5/sub-5_2019-11-01 ACh sensor staining in SMG 02 - Same Thresholds_z14.tif"]
                  + sorted(f["path"] for f in X.manifest("108")["files"] if "/sub-1/" in f["path"]),
           "75": ["files/dataset_description.xlsx", "files/subjects.xlsx"]
                 + sorted(f["path"] for f in X.manifest("75")["files"] if f["path"].endswith(".lsm"))}
    return {f"{ds}/{p}": X.entry(ds, p) for ds, ps in out.items() for p in ps}

FILES = files_read()
for key, f in FILES.items():
    print(f"SPARC:{key}  {f['size']:>11,d} B  sha256 {X.sha_hex(*key.split('/', 1))}")

Data check¶

What each dataset holds, read from its manifest, its SDS sheets and the files themselves. Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output.

for ds in ("108", "75"):
    m = X.manifest(ds)
    files = m["files"]
    print(f"SPARC:{ds} version {m['version']} ({X.DATASETS[ds]['doi']}), published {m['datePublished']}: {m['name']}")
    print(f"  {len(files)} files, {sum(f['size'] for f in files) / 1e9:.3f} GB")
    folders = pd.Series(["/".join(f["path"].split("/")[:4]) if f["path"].startswith("files/primary")
                         else "/".join(f["path"].split("/")[:2]) for f in files])
    print(folders.value_counts().sort_index().to_string(), "\n")

for ds in ("108", "75"):
    dd = pd.read_excel(io.BytesIO(X.read_bytes(ds, "files/dataset_description.xlsx")), header=None)
    dd = dd.set_index(0)
    for key in ("Originating Article DOI", "Number of subjects", "Number of samples", "Protocol URL or DOI"):
        vals = [str(v) for v in dd.loc[key].iloc[2:].tolist() if str(v) != "nan"]
        print(f"SPARC:{ds} dataset_description {key}: {vals}")
    sub = pd.read_excel(io.BytesIO(X.read_bytes(ds, "files/subjects.xlsx"))).dropna(how="all", axis=1)
    print(f"SPARC:{ds} subjects.xlsx, every column:")
    print(sub.to_string(index=False), "\n")

SPARC:108 has six subjects in subjects.xlsx, with their experiment groups (calibration curve, dose-dependent stimulation, sensor staining, inhibitor), and states 6 subjects; SPARC:75 has one ChAT(BAC)-eGFP mouse and one sample. SPARC:108 names only the bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2020.07.06.189696) as its originating article, not the PNAS paper; SPARC:75 names none. The next cell compares the primary folder's manifest.xlsx with the files that are there.

The primary manifest.xlsx describes the files under names that differ from the deposited ones (for example sub-1/0.000714_uM.tif in the sheet, sub-1/sub-1_0.000714 uM in the dataset, which also lacks the .tif extension for seven of the eight calibration files), so no file is described by its own name. The sheet's descriptions of the sub-1 files say "ACh release by electrical stimulation", while the README, the subjects sheet ("calibration curve") and the paper make them the ex vivo calibration with added ACh.

In vivo recordings¶

Each recording is read once; the analyses below use only the reduced traces kept here: the mean over the stained tissue (Otsu threshold of the mean pre-stimulus image), the mean over the whole frame, and the mean of each 40 x 40 pixel block inside the tissue.

In [5]:
V = {}
rows = []
MAPS = {}   # block onset/peak maps of the pHAb half of sub-2 and sub-3 (fig7 and figs12), under each variant
for key in X.MOVIES:
    m = X.movie(key)
    rec = {"shape": m["shape"], "times": m["times"], "acquired": m["acquired"]}
    for h, a in m["halves"].items():
        mean_img = a[:X.STIM_FRAME].mean(0)
        mask = X.tissue_mask(mean_img)
        bt, org = X.blocks(a, mask)
        sat = a.max(0) >= 65534
        rec[h] = {"mean_img": mean_img, "mask": mask, "tissue": a[:, mask].mean(1),
                  "tissue_unsat": a[:, mask & ~sat].mean(1), "sat_px_frac": float((mask & sat).sum() / mask.sum()),
                  "full": a.reshape(len(a), -1).mean(1), "blocks": bt, "origins": org,
                  "dark": float(np.percentile(mean_img, 0.1))}
        if h == "right" and key in ("sub-2 3V", "sub-3 8V"):
            for size in (16, 32):
                for k in (2.0, 3.0, 5.0):
                    for fit, after in (("a", 120.0), ("c", 180.0), ("b", None)):
                        MAPS[(key, size, k, fit)] = X.block_onsets(a, mask, X.STIM_FRAME, size, k, after)
        dt = np.diff(m["times"]) if len(m["times"]) > 1 else np.array([np.nan])
        rows.append({"recording": key, "acquired": m["acquired"][:30], "frames": a.shape[0], "frame_px": f"{a.shape[1]}x{a.shape[2]}",
                     "channel": h, "timestamps": len(m["times"]), "dt_median_s": np.median(dt), "dt_min": dt.min(), "dt_max": dt.max(),
                     "min": int(a.min()), "max": int(a.max()), "dark (0.1th pct of mean image)": round(rec[h]["dark"]),
                     "tissue mean (pre-onset)": round(float(mean_img[mask].mean())), "off-tissue median": round(float(np.median(mean_img[~mask]))),
                     "saturated_px_frames_%": round(100 * (a >= 65534).mean(), 2),
                     "tissue_px_ever_saturated_%": round(100 * rec[h]["sat_px_frac"], 1),
                     "tissue_frac": round(mask.mean(), 2), "blocks": len(bt)})
    if "left" in rec and "right" in rec:
        rec["left"]["by_right_mask"] = m["halves"]["left"][:, rec["right"]["mask"]].mean(1)
    V[key] = rec
    del m, a
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print(f"block maps computed: {len(MAPS)}; peak memory {rss_mb():.0f} MB, {time.time() - T0:.0f} s")

Frames are 16-bit counts from a Hamamatsu C11440-22C camera (binning 4, 50 ms exposure); the files carry no spatial scale (their calibration is in pixels). sub-2 and sub-3 keep both W-VIEW GEMINI channels side by side (512 x 512) and a timestamp per frame: the interval is 0.50 s (one 0.60 s gap after the first frame), not the 0.55 s the paper states for its sampling. sub-4 and sub-6 were saved by ImageJ, cropped to one channel, with only the first frame's timestamp, so their interval cannot be read from the files. No file labels its channels; which half is pHAb is settled below from the response. Pixels at the top of the 16-bit range (65534 and above) are saturated: in the right half of sub-2 and sub-3 and in both sub-6 files a share of the tissue pixels saturate at some frame (printed), so their responses are clipped. The analyses of sub-6 show the tissue without those pixels as a further ROI.

Dark level. No background or camera offset is subtracted in the paper's Methods, and none is subtracted here in the main readings. The darkest pixels of each mean image (0.1th percentile, printed as "dark") sit at 1,574 to 1,643 counts in sub-2, sub-3 and sub-4 and at 2,641 and 2,941 in the two sub-6 files, near the lowest pixel of each file, so they are the floor of the camera, not tissue; the pixels outside the tissue mask of sub-2 and sub-3 are far brighter (printed), as the field is all ganglion and glow. The dark level is 4 to 10% of the tissue means of sub-2, sub-3 and sub-6, so subtracting it would raise their dF/F by about that share; fig5b-in-vivo-response shows the tissue ROI with it subtracted as a variant. In sub-4 the tissue mean is close to the dark level, so its dF/F would change several-fold; sub-4 is used by no tested claim.

def z_from_pre(tr, n_pre=X.STIM_FRAME):
    pre = tr[:n_pre]
    return (tr - pre.mean()) / pre.std()

Clock. The files do not record when the stimulation was given. The paper puts its start at 10.45 s in Fig. 6A and Fig. 7A, frame 19 on its 0.55 s clock (STIM_FRAME). In sub-2, sub-3 and sub-6 after washout each tissue trace departs from baseline (|z| > 5 against frames 0 to 18) 4 to 13 frames after frame 19, at frame 23 to 34. In sub-3 (8 V) the first change is a drop in both channels, followed by the rise in one. With the drug, sub-6 has no frame with |z| > 5 and rises by at most 3.3%. sub-4 (10 V) first departs at frame 55, so its stimulation did not start at 10.45 s; it is used by no tested claim. Its whole trace (printed and plotted) holds one response: one peak of 8.7% at frame 99, with |z| > 5 from frame 78 to 210 and the signal near or below baseline before and after. It holds no repeated stimulations, so fig5e-reversibility cannot be tested on it, and no 3 V or 5 V recording of the same ganglion exists for fig5c-voltage-dose. That the responses start after frame 19 is consistent with the stated onset; it does not prove it.

Channels. In sub-2 and sub-3 the right half rises after stimulation (by 27.1% and 48.1% over the tissue) and the left half does not rise above its baseline; the right half is taken as pHAb and the left as AF647. The files do not label them, so this is an assumption, and figs16-af647-stable rests on it. (While preparing, outside this notebook, the time-lapse panels of Fig. 7A, the nanosensor signal of the 8 V recording, were compared with sub-3 and match its right half; this is not run here, as the entry reads no figures. It does not decide the channels, which rest on which half rises.)

Recordings deposited twice. The next cell compares the mean images.

from skimage.registration import phase_cross_correlation

def aligned_r(a, b):
    h, w = min(a.shape[0], b.shape[0]), min(a.shape[1], b.shape[1])
    a, b = a[:h, :w], b[:h, :w]
    shift = phase_cross_correlation(a, b, upsample_factor=1)[0]
    b2 = ndi.shift(b, shift, order=1)
    sl = (slice(20, h - 20), slice(20, w - 20))
    return shift, stats.pearsonr(a[sl].ravel(), b2[sl].ravel())[0]

pairs = [("sub-2 3V", "right", "sub-3 8V", "right"), ("sub-2 3V", "left", "sub-3 8V", "left"),
         ("sub-6 with drug", "single", "sub-6 without drug", "single"),
         ("sub-2 3V", "right", "sub-6 without drug", "single"), ("sub-2 3V", "right", "sub-4 10V", "single"),
         ("sub-3 8V", "right", "sub-4 10V", "single")]
for k1, h1, k2, h2 in pairs:
    s, r = aligned_r(V[k1][h1]["mean_img"], V[k2][h2]["mean_img"])
    print(f"{k1} {h1} vs {k2} {h2}: shift {s}, r = {r:.3f}")
print("acquired:", {k: V[k]["acquired"][:40] for k in V})
print("traces identical between any two recordings:",
      any(np.array_equal(V[a][ha]["tissue"], V[b][hb]["tissue"]) for a, ha, b, hb in pairs))

sub-2 (3 V) and sub-3 (8 V) were recorded 14 minutes apart on the same day and their mean images match with no shift (r = 0.93 for the right halves), far more closely than images of different recordings do (r = 0.06 to 0.47): they are two stimulations of one ganglion. The paper says the AQuA analysis used one mouse stimulated at 3 V and 8 V (Methods, AQuA Analysis); the subjects sheet lists sub-2 and sub-3 as two subjects. Neither recording is a copy of the other (the traces differ), so each is used once. The two sub-6 files are one field before and after washout, as the paper's Fig. 6 describes.

Eight recordings of one mouse (sub-1), each 22 to 34 frames of one channel cropped to 509 x 255 pixels, acquired in increasing concentration over two hours on one day. The concentrations in the names (0.000714 to 714 uM) are the paper's final concentrations (stock divided by 1.4, Methods); the paper's range runs to 7.14 mM, and the deposit has 8 concentrations and one of three mice. The files keep only the first frame's timestamp, so their frame interval is not recorded; the time of ACh addition is not recorded either. Six of the eight recordings rise by 19.8 to 58.4% within one frame, at frame 7 to 9; at 0.00714 and 0.0714 uM the largest one-frame rise is 1.7 and 3.0%, with no clear step. The channel is not labelled; it is taken as pHAb, the channel the calibration measures. The traces (plotted and printed) show the shape of each: in the six recordings with a step, the signal drifts down by 1.5 to 15.5% over the frames before it, then jumps within one frame and stays high to the end; the 0.00714 uM recording ends with one frame at -39.6%.

The LSM files of SPARC:75 name their dyes: GFP and AF647 in the BTX stacks; AF488 (GFP), AF647 and AF546 (pHAb) in the nanosensor images. In the high-magnification BTX stack only the first planes hold data; the others (count printed) are all zero, so the stack is 62 planes of 0.1 um by its metadata but about 1.2 um of tissue in fact. The nanosensor images are single planes. The sub-5 CZI holds 27 planes of three channels (AF647, AF532 for pHAb, EGFP), with a 17.41 um stack, as the Methods state (27 slices, 17.41 um, lasers 488, 514 and 633 nm). The 27 per-plane TIFFs of sub-5 are 8-bit RGB renders of the same stack (the printed correlations match each colour to one CZI channel), so the stack is deposited twice (three times with the derivative OME-TIFF and JPX); the CZI is used.

The HPLC files have no header. The first column runs to 44.7 min at a constant step, so it is time in minutes, not volume; the paper reports volumes and does not give the flow rate. The UV-Vis workbooks hold spectra titled "sensor" (eight repeats, a reblank and water) and one of the DNA scaffold; there are no spectra of pure AChE or BTX, which fig2g-conjugation-ratios needs. The three gel images are 2048 x 2048 16-bit scans (ethidium bromide, pHAb, AF647).

fig2d-hplc-yield¶

In size-exclusion HPLC the assembled nanosensors elute first (main peak near 7.5 mL), followed by a second peak at 9.1 to 9.2 mL of unreacted material, and the nanosensors are about 77% of the reaction mixture by area under all peaks of the pHAb channel.

Criterion: the area of the first peak over the summed area of all detectable peaks of the pHAb chromatogram, (a) limits at the minima between peaks with a flat baseline at the pre-injection level, (b) the same with a linear baseline under each peak; share 69.3 to 84.7%, main peak 6.75 to 8.25 mL, second peak 8.19 to 10.12 mL.

Details not in the claims file. "Detectable" is taken as a prominence of at least 1% of the largest peak (0.5% as a variant), a choice made here. The start of the first peak is where the signal rises above the pre-injection level plus 3 SD (the first 5 min, before any peak). The end of the last peak is open, and three ends are run: (i) where the signal returns to the pre-injection level plus 3 SD; (ii) the end of the peak's own descent, the first point after it where the slope (101-sample running mean) falls below 1% of the steepest slope of the chromatogram; (iii) where the signal falls below 2% of the peak's height. Ends (ii) and (iii) leave out the low tail after about 21 min, which (i) gives to the second peak. Reading (b) is run as written (a line under each peak, from its limits) and as a common line from the start of the first peak to the end of the last, with a vertical drop at the valley, the usual way to split two overlapping peaks on a sloped baseline; a line under each peak alone cuts through the second peak, as its left limit is the valley.

The file gives time, not volume, and the paper gives no flow rate (Methods, "Superdex 200 increase 10/300 GL column ... via HPLC (Infinity 1260, Agilent)"; no rate is stated anywhere in the text or SI). The retention volumes therefore cannot be tested: any rate could be chosen to put the main peak at 7.5 mL. Only the ratio of the two retention times, which does not depend on the rate, is compared with the paper's 9.1 to 9.2 over 7.5 mL. The rate that would put the main peak at 7.5 mL is printed for information.

from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter1d

t, y = X.hplc("PHAB")
pre = t < 5
base, base_sd = np.median(y[pre]), y[pre].std()
print(f"pre-injection level {base:.4f} (SD {base_sd:.4f}) over the first 5 min")
slope = np.gradient(uniform_filter1d(y, 101), t)

def peak_limits(y, peaks, level, end):
    lims = []
    i = peaks[0]
    while i > 0 and y[i] > level:
        i -= 1
    lims.append(i)
    for a, b in zip(peaks[:-1], peaks[1:]):
        lims.append(a + int(np.argmin(y[a:b])))
    i = peaks[-1]
    if end == "i return to pre-injection + 3 SD":
        while i < len(y) - 1 and y[i] > level:
            i += 1
    elif end == "ii end of descent (slope < 1% of steepest)":
        i = i + int(np.argmax((np.arange(len(y))[i:] > i + 50) & (np.abs(slope[i:]) < 0.01 * np.abs(slope).max())))
    else:
        i = i + int(np.argmax(y[i:] - base < 0.02 * (y[i] - base)))
    lims.append(i)
    return lims

rows = []
for detect in (0.01, 0.005):
    pk, pr = find_peaks(y, prominence=detect * (y.max() - base))
    # the end readings apply to the end of the second peak; with the 0.5% rule a third, late peak is counted with limits (i)
    for end in ("i return to pre-injection + 3 SD", "ii end of descent (slope < 1% of steepest)", "iii below 2% of the peak height"):
        s0, v0, e0 = peak_limits(y, pk[:2], base + 3 * base_sd, end)
        segs = [(s0, v0), (v0, e0)]
        for p in pk[2:]:   # a later, separate peak (0.5% rule): its own limits by reading (i)
            s3, e3 = peak_limits(y, [p], base + 3 * base_sd, "i return to pre-injection + 3 SD")
            segs.append((max(s3, e0), e3))
        flat = [np.trapezoid(y[a:b + 1] - base, t[a:b + 1]) for a, b in segs]
        each = [np.trapezoid(y[a:b + 1] - np.interp(t[a:b + 1], [t[a], t[b]], [y[a], y[b]]), t[a:b + 1]) for a, b in segs]
        common_line = lambda tt: np.interp(tt, [t[s0], t[e0]], [y[s0], y[e0]])
        common = [np.trapezoid(y[a:b + 1] - common_line(t[a:b + 1]), t[a:b + 1]) for a, b in segs[:2]] + \
                 [np.trapezoid(y[a:b + 1] - np.interp(t[a:b + 1], [t[a], t[b]], [y[a], y[b]]), t[a:b + 1]) for a, b in segs[2:]]
        for reading, areas in (("a flat baseline", flat), ("b line under each peak", each), ("b common line, drop at valley", common)):
            rows.append({"detectable": f"{detect:.1%}", "end of 2nd peak": end, "reading": reading, "peaks (min)": np.round(t[pk], 2).tolist(),
                         "limits (min)": [round(float(t[a]), 2) for a, b in segs] + [round(float(t[segs[-1][1]]), 2)],
                         "areas": np.round(areas, 2).tolist(), "main share (%)": round(100 * areas[0] / sum(areas), 1)})
H = pd.DataFrame(rows)
H["share_ok"] = (H["main share (%)"] - 77).abs() <= 7.7

Result: partially reproduced, resting on an assumption about where the second peak ends. The pHAb chromatogram has two detectable peaks, at 15.16 and 18.05 min (a third, small one at 37.27 min passes the 0.5% rule). The share of the first peak depends on the reading. With a flat baseline (reading a) it is 65.8 to 68.2% under every end of the second peak, below the tolerance of 69.3 to 84.7%; so is a common line under both peaks with a drop at the valley (66.2 to 69.1%). With a line under each peak (reading b, as the criterion writes it), the share is 77.5 to 83.1%, within tolerance, when the second peak ends where its own descent ends (end ii, 20.53 min) or where it falls below 2% of its height (end iii, 20.94 min); when it ends where the signal returns to the pre-injection level (end i, 29.76 min), the line from the valley (5.19 high, at 17.27 min) runs above the low tail and the second area is negative, which is no share. From 21 to 30 min the signal is 0.055 to 0.250, 1.3 to 5.9 times the pre-injection level, against a main peak of 13.62; end (i) counts that tail in the second peak. Ends (ii) and (iii), where a peak's own descent ends, are the usual limits of a peak, so the share holds under reading (b), 4 of 18 readings in all. That reading has a cost: as the valley is high, the line under each peak cuts through both peaks, keeping 54% of the main peak's area above the flat baseline and 30% (end ii) or 23% (end iii) of the second peak's. Every reading that splits the overlap the usual way (a flat baseline, or a common line with a drop at the valley) gives 65.8 to 69.1%, just below the tolerance. The share therefore holds by the letter of the criterion's reading (b) only. The retention volumes cannot be tested: the paper gives no flow rate, and the rate that would put the main peak at 7.5 mL (0.495 mL/min) is read from the data. The ratio of the two retention times, 1.191, is 1.8% below the paper's 1.213 to 1.227. Partially reproduced: the share holds under one reading of the criterion, a reading that cuts away part of each peak, and the volume part cannot be tested.

fig2e-page-bands¶

In native PAGE the purified nanosensor runs as several bands of lower mobility than the DNA scaffold (likely 1 to 4 AChE per scaffold), and these bands carry both pHAb and AF647 fluorescence.

Criterion: lane 3 (main peak) shows at least two bands above the scaffold band of lane 1 (ethidium bromide, Fig. 2E), with signal above the lane background in both the pHAb and AF647 images (Fig. S2C); judged by eye with lane profiles. Lanes are found as runs of columns with signal (lane_segments); bands are peaks of the lane profile with a prominence of at least 5% of its range (bands), a choice made here. The ethidium image is framed differently from the two fluorescence images, which are registered to each other (shift printed); band positions are therefore compared within the ethidium image, and within the pair of fluorescence images, where the scaffold band of lane 1 (pHAb-labelled DNA) is the reference.

        prof, bl = describe(G[c], seg, fl_y0, fl_y1, c)
        fl[(i + 1, c)] = (prof, bl)
        print(f"  lane {i + 1} {c:5s} {seg}: {bl}")
for c in ("PHAB", "AF652"):
    g = gap(G[c]) - np.median(G[c])
    print(f"  {c} background between lanes 1 and 2: mean {g.mean():.0f}, SD {g.std():.0f}")

fl_scaffold = max([b for b in fl[(1, "PHAB")][1] if b[0] > fl_well], key=lambda b: b[1])[0]
print(f"pHAb lane 1 band (pHAb-labelled scaffold) at row {fl_scaffold}")
ph3 = [b for b in fl[(3, "PHAB")][1] if fl_well < b[0] < fl_scaffold - 10]
af3_prof = fl[(3, "AF652")][0]
af_bg = gap(G["AF652"]) - np.median(G["AF652"])
for r, v, p in ph3:
    af_v = af3_prof[r - fl_y0]
    af_near = [b for b in fl[(3, "AF652")][1] if abs(b[0] - r) <= 10]
    print(f"  lane 3 pHAb band at row {r} (signal {v}); AF647 there {af_v:.0f} = {af_v / max(af_bg.std(), 1):.0f} SD of the gap; AF647 band within 10 rows: {af_near}")

for a_, (img, lanes, y0, y1, title) in zip(ax, [(G["eb"], eb_lanes, eb_y0, eb_y1, "ethidium"), (G["PHAB"], fl_lanes, fl_y0, fl_y1, "pHAb"), (G["AF652"], fl_lanes, fl_y0, fl_y1, "AF647")]):

In the fluorescence images, lane 3 has two pHAb bands (rows 783 and 861) above the pHAb-labelled scaffold band of lane 1 (row 1119), and the AF647 image has bands at the same rows (783 and 859), 8 and 10 SD above the gel between lanes. Lane 1 of the fluorescence images has one pHAb band and no AF647 band above the background (its largest AF647 peak is 765 counts above the image median, against an SD of 1231 between lanes), as for a DNA scaffold without BTX: Figure 2E labels lane 1 as the scaffold, Figure S2C as unpurified nanosensor.

figs5-btx-staining¶

Ex vivo staining of freshly isolated SMG with BTX-AF647 shows a punctate pattern across the ganglion, confirming nicotinic ACh receptors on SMG neurons.

Criterion: in the confocal z-stacks of a ChAT(BAC)-eGFP SMG (Fig. S5), the AF647 channel shows discrete puncta distributed over the ganglion and lying on or next to GFP-positive cell bodies; judged by eye on maximum projections and single slices. The numbers below support the judgement: AF647 puncta (components above the background threshold, 0.1 to 25 um^2, puncta; the background rule is in xia2021.py: since round 1 of verification the median plus 3 SD of the lower half of the pixels reflected about the median, with the first rule, the mean plus 3 SD of the lower half, shown as a variant, as it passes much of the noise), their density, the share of 8 x 8 tiles over the ganglion (GFP mask) that hold one, and the share lying within 1 um of the GFP mask, against the share of the field that lies there (the value for puncta placed at random). The GFP mask is drawn two ways (soma_mask): Otsu's threshold, which in these images picks out the bright presynaptic fibres more than the dimmer somata, and the background rule, which takes in the somata. Single planes: the plane with the brightest AF647.

def punctum_stats(af, gfp, px, label, rule="reflected"):
    lab, keep, thr = X.puncta(af, px, rule=rule)
    cents = np.round(np.array(ndi.center_of_mass(np.ones_like(lab), lab, keep))).astype(int) if len(keep) else np.zeros((0, 2), int)
    h, w = af.shape
    out = {"image": label, "background rule": rule, "threshold": round(thr), "puncta": len(keep), "per_100um2": round(100 * len(keep) / (h * w * px ** 2), 2)}
    for rule in ("otsu", "background"):
        gm = X.soma_mask(gfp, px, rule)
        near = ndi.binary_dilation(gm, iterations=max(1, int(round(1.0 / px))))
        tiles, filled = 0, 0
        for i in range(8):
            for j in range(8):
                sl = (slice(i * h // 8, (i + 1) * h // 8), slice(j * w // 8, (j + 1) * w // 8))
                if gm[sl].mean() > 0.2:
                    tiles += 1
                    filled += int(np.any((cents[:, 0] >= sl[0].start) & (cents[:, 0] < sl[0].stop) & (cents[:, 1] >= sl[1].start) & (cents[:, 1] < sl[1].stop)))
        out[f"GFP mask ({rule}) frac"] = round(float(gm.mean()), 2)
        out[f"tiles over GFP with puncta ({rule})"] = f"{filled}/{tiles}"
        out[f"puncta within 1 um ({rule})"] = round(float(near[cents[:, 0], cents[:, 1]].mean()), 2) if len(keep) else np.nan
        out[f"field within 1 um ({rule})"] = round(float(near.mean()), 2)
    return out

Result: reproduced. By eye, on the maximum projections above and on single planes, the AF647 (BTX) signal is punctate, with puncta over the whole ganglion and along the borders of the GFP-positive somata. In numbers, with the background rule used since round 1 (reflected), every 8 x 8 tile over the GFP mask holds puncta in all four images (5/5 to 29/29 tiles with the Otsu mask), at 4.4 to 15.8 puncta per 100 um^2 (17.8 to 64.4 with the first rule, which passed much of the noise). Nearness to GFP beyond chance holds in three of the four images by at least one mask: in the low-magnification projection 0.82 of puncta lie within 1 um of the Otsu GFP mask, against 0.37 of the field (0.29 against 0.11 with the background-rule mask); in its brightest plane 0.61 against 0.24 (background-rule mask); in the high-magnification projection 0.18 against 0.15 and 0.12 against 0.09. The high-magnification stack holds data in 12 of its 62 planes (50 are all zero). The judgement by eye decides the outcome; the numbers support it.

fig3d-sensor-on-soma¶

Confocal imaging of a nanosensor-stained SMG shows punctate AF647 and pHAb staining that overlaps and lies mainly on the neuronal cell soma, consistent with the BTX staining.

Criterion: in the confocal stacks of a nanosensor-injected, fixed ChAT(BAC)-eGFP SMG, puncta in the AF647 and pHAb channels coincide and most lie on GFP-positive somata; (a) judged by eye, as the paper does; (b) as a check, more than half of the AF647 puncta (threshold at mean plus 3 SD of the background) overlap pHAb puncta and lie within the GFP soma mask. Reproduced when (a) holds; (b) is shown. The background of the threshold is not defined in the paper; the rule used since round 1 of verification is the median plus 3 SD of the lower half of the pixels reflected about the median (X.background_threshold), and the first rule (mean plus 3 SD of the lower half), which marked a third or more of the field and so made overlap near certain, is shown as a variant. The images: the sub-5 stack of SPARC:108 (maximum projection and middle plane), and the three high-magnification nanosensor images of SPARC:75. A punctum overlaps pHAb when one of its pixels is above the pHAb threshold. As the pHAb channel also shows the GFP of the somata (see the correlation printed), a variant uses the pHAb channel after a white top-hat of radius 1 um, which keeps spots and removes the broad soma signal. As a reference for chance, the overlap is also computed with the pHAb mask shifted by 5 um (a deterministic shift, about a third of a soma; the larger of two diagonal shifts is printed), for the plain and the top-hat pHAb masks. A full-resolution crop shows each channel alone. "Within the soma mask" is shown with the Otsu mask, the same grown by 1 um (BTX binds the soma membrane at its edge), and the background-rule mask; each is compared with the share of the field the mask covers.

from skimage.morphology import disk, white_tophat

def overlap_stats(af, ph, gfp, px, label, rule="reflected"):
    lab, keep, thr = X.puncta(af, px, rule=rule)
    r1 = max(1, int(round(1.0 / px)))
    ph_th = white_tophat(ph, disk(r1))
    pm = ph > X.background_threshold(ph, rule=rule)
    pm_th = ph_th > X.background_threshold(ph_th, rule=rule)
    gm = X.soma_mask(gfp, px)
    gm1 = ndi.binary_dilation(gm, iterations=r1)
    gmb = X.soma_mask(gfp, px, "background")
    idx = ndi.labeled_comprehension
    sh = int(round(5.0 / px))
    ov = lambda m: idx(m, lab, keep, np.any, bool, False) if len(keep) else np.array([], bool)
    o, o_th = ov(pm), ov(pm_th)
    null = lambda m: max(ov(np.roll(m, (sh, sh), (0, 1))).mean(), ov(np.roll(m, (-sh, sh), (0, 1))).mean())
    cents = np.round(np.array(ndi.center_of_mass(np.ones_like(lab), lab, keep))).astype(int) if len(keep) else np.zeros((0, 2), int)
    ins, ins1, insb = (g_[cents[:, 0], cents[:, 1]] for g_ in (gm, gm1, gmb))
    return {"image": label, "background rule": rule, "AF647 puncta": len(keep), "AF647>thr area": round(float((af > thr).mean()), 3),
            "pHAb>thr area": round(float(pm.mean()), 3), "overlap pHAb": round(o.mean(), 2), "overlap, pHAb shifted 5 um (larger of 2)": round(null(pm), 2),
            "pHAb top-hat>thr area": round(float(pm_th.mean()), 3), "overlap pHAb top-hat": round(o_th.mean(), 2),
            "overlap top-hat, shifted 5 um (larger of 2)": round(null(pm_th), 2),
            "in soma mask (Otsu)": round(ins.mean(), 2), "soma mask frac": round(gm.mean(), 2),
            "within 1 um of soma": round(ins1.mean(), 2), "soma+1um frac": round(gm1.mean(), 2),
            "in soma (background rule)": round(insb.mean(), 2), "soma (background rule) frac": round(float(gmb.mean()), 2),
            "coinciding puncta within 1 um of soma": round(ins1[o].mean(), 2) if o.any() else np.nan,
            "(b) both, mask": round((o & ins).mean(), 2), "(b) both, top-hat, +1um": round((o_th & ins1).mean(), 2),
            "(b) both, background-rule mask": round((o & insb).mean(), 2),
            "r pHAb vs GFP": round(stats.pearsonr(ph[::3, ::3].ravel(), gfp[::3, ::3].ravel())[0], 2)}

Result: partially reproduced. By eye (merges above, and the full-resolution crop with each channel shown alone), the sub-5 stack shows puncta in both channels and yellow spots where they coincide, as in Fig. 3D; but much of the AF647 signal lines the borders of the cells and the capsule of the ganglion, and the coinciding spots lie mostly between or at the edges of the somata. With the background rule used since round 1 (reflected), which marks 7 to 12% of the field as pHAb in four of the five images (35% in sub-5 plane 13), the coincidence is above chance: 59 to 85% of AF647 puncta overlap pHAb in those four, against 39 to 53% with the pHAb mask shifted by 5 um (top-hat pHAb: 68 to 79% against 40 to 64%); in plane 13 it is 98% against 95%. The first rule marked 32 to 48% of the field and gave 84 to 98% against 78 to 98%. The soma localisation is not shown: 9 to 47% of AF647 puncta lie in the Otsu soma mask, which covers 23 to 42% of the field, and 15 to 52% of the coinciding puncta lie within 1 um of it, against 27 to 48% of the field. Reading (b) fails: the share of AF647 puncta that overlap pHAb and lie in the soma mask is 0.09 to 0.35 (0.13 to 0.40 with the top-hat and the 1 um margin), below one half in every image. In the sub-5 stack the pHAb channel correlates with GFP (r 0.43 and 0.53), so part of its signal inside somata may be GFP excited at 514 nm. Partially reproduced: the puncta coincide beyond chance, but their place on the somata is not shown.

fig4b-michaelis-menten¶

The initial rate of the ex vivo nanosensor response follows a Michaelis-Menten curve in ACh concentration with EC50 (Km) 49.24 ± 5.84 uM and Vmax 281.00 ± 7.14 %/s (R2 0.9811); the upper limit of detection is 358.01 uM.

Criterion: initial rates of pHAb dF/F per concentration, fit by V = Vmax [ACh] / (Km + [ACh]); reproduced when Km (43.40 to 55.08 uM) and Vmax (273.86 to 288.14 %/s) are within tolerance under one reading. Readings run here, all crossed: frame interval 0.55 s (paper) or 0.50 s (the in vivo files); photobleaching curve fit to (a) the frames before onset (there is no recovery within these recordings) or (b) the whole trace; baseline (a) mean of the frames before onset or (b) the first frame; initial rate (a) a linear fit from onset to the peak or (b) over the first k = 2 to 5 frames; ROI the stained tissue or the whole frame (the paper's ROI is not given). Onset is the last frame before the largest one-frame rise, as the addition time is not recorded (an assumption; at 0.00714 and 0.0714 uM there is no clear step); a variant puts it at one frame for every recording. Means over mice and all points are the same here (one mouse). Upper limit of detection: (a) the concentration at 88% of Vmax, (b) the upper end of the region where the tangent at EC50 (on log concentration) stays within 5% of the curve (Methods, "within 5% deviation").

def ulod(vmax, km):
    a = km * 0.88 / (1 - 0.88)
    cs = np.logspace(np.log10(km), np.log10(km) + 4, 4000)
    tang = vmax / 2 + vmax / 4 * np.log(cs / km)
    mm = X.michaelis_menten(cs, vmax, km)
    ok = np.abs(tang - mm) / mm <= 0.05
    b = cs[np.argmin(ok)] if not ok.all() else np.nan
    return a, b
for label, (vm, k) in (("paper's fit", (281.0, 49.24)), ("first reading", (main.Vmax, main.Km_uM))):
    a, b = ulod(vm, k)
    print(f"upper limit of detection, {label}: (a) 88% of Vmax at {a:.4g} uM; (b) tangent within 5% up to {b:.4g} uM")

Result: not reproduced. No reading gives Km or Vmax within tolerance (0 of 80). Over all readings Km is 0.031 to 0.73 uM, against 49.24 ± 5.84 uM, Vmax 8.3 to 49.7 %/s, against 281.00 ± 7.14 %/s, and R2 0.01 to 0.73, against 0.9811. In the first reading the rates are 0.3 to 16.3 %/s and do not rise steadily with concentration (Spearman rho 0.54, p 0.168); in the data check the one-frame step is 23.1% at 0.000714 uM and 19.8% at 0.714 uM, 41.9% at 7.14 uM and 38.4% at 714 uM, and there is no clear step at 0.00714 and 0.0714 uM. The onset rests on an assumption (the frame before the largest one-frame rise), and the traces printed in the data check show why it is weak: in the six recordings with a step the signal falls by 1.5 to 15.5% over the frames before it (most at 7.14 uM), then jumps within one frame to a plateau, and the 0.000714 uM recording steps by more than the 0.714 uM one. Dips and steps of this kind may come from adding the solution as much as from the sensor, which the files cannot tell. With one onset for every recording (frame 7, the most common), Km is 0.545 uM and Vmax 11.4 %/s, still far from the paper. The upper limit of detection of the first reading's fit is 1.92 uM by (a) and 0.96 uM by (b); the paper's own constants give 361.1 uM by (a), close to its 358.01 uM, and 181.3 uM by (b). The deposit holds one of the three mice and 8 concentrations, so this is not the paper's fit; the rates of this mouse do not follow the paper's curve under any reading run here.

fig4b-lod¶

The lower limit of detection is 228 nM, where two regression lines through the low-concentration data (0.71 nM to 14.28 uM) cross; the theoretical response there from the Michaelis-Menten equation (1.3 %/s, 0.72% per 0.55 s frame) is 8.18 times the background noise of 0.088 ± 0.039%.

Criterion: readings (a) the split of the points into two runs that minimises the summed squared residuals of two lines, on linear concentration, (b) the same on log10 concentration, (c) the split of Fig. 4B(ii) as read from its lines. Reading (c) is not run: it needs the figure, which the entry does not read. The rates are those of fig4b-michaelis-menten, under each of its readings; the deposit has five concentrations up to 14.28 uM (0.000714 to 7.14 uM). Reproduced when the crossing is within 205.2 to 250.8 nM under one reading. Noise: (a) SD of the photobleaching-corrected dF/F of the baseline frames, (b) mean absolute frame-to-frame change of that dF/F; the signal-to-noise ratio is the theoretical response at the crossing (the first reading's fit, times 0.55 s) over the noise.

        if best is None:

    tr, on = c["tissue"], c["onset"]
    corr, _ = X.bleach_correct(tr, np.arange(on + 1))
    d = X.dff(corr, on, "mean")[:on + 1]
    noise_sd.append(d.std()); noise_step.append(np.abs(np.diff(d)).mean())
noise_sd, noise_step = np.array(noise_sd), np.array(noise_step)
print(f"\nbaseline noise (a) SD of dF/F: mean {noise_sd.mean():.3f} ± {noise_sd.std():.3f}% over 8 recordings ({np.round(noise_sd, 3).tolist()})")
print(f"baseline noise (b) mean |frame-to-frame change|: mean {noise_step.mean():.3f} ± {noise_step.std():.3f}%")
xc = float(first.crossing_nM.iloc[0]) / 1000 if len(first) else np.nan
for label, (vm, k, at) in (("paper's fit at 228 nM", (281.0, 49.24, 0.228)), ("first reading's fit at its crossing", (main.Vmax, main.Km_uM, xc))):
    resp = X.michaelis_menten(at, vm, k) * 0.55
    print(f"{label}: theoretical response {resp:.3f}% per 0.55 s; SNR (a) {resp / noise_sd.mean():.2f}, (b) {resp / noise_step.mean():.2f}")

Result: not reproduced. None of the 160 crossings (80 rate readings, on linear and on log concentration) falls within 205.2 to 250.8 nM; their medians are -140 nM on linear concentration (a crossing outside the data) and 3.11 nM on log concentration, and the first reading gives 0.977 nM. The baseline noise is 1.77 ± 2.34% by its SD (a) and 1.17 ± 0.95% by the frame-to-frame change (b), 20 and 13 times the paper's 0.088%; at these levels the paper's own theoretical response at 228 nM (0.712% per 0.55 s) would have a signal-to-noise ratio of 0.40 or 0.61, not 8.18. The fit of this mouse gives 0.018% per frame at its crossing (signal-to-noise 0.01 to 0.02). Reading (c), the split of Fig. 4B(ii), is not run, as the entry reads no figures; with rates that do not rise with concentration below 14.28 uM (fig4b-michaelis-menten) a crossing near 228 nM under it is not expected, but that is not shown here.

fig5b-in-vivo-response¶

In vivo, lingual nerve stimulation (3 V, 10 Hz, 10 ms, 100 pulses) raises nanosensor fluorescence by 3.7% by 15 s with initial rate 0.294 ± 0.116 %/s, recovering to baseline within 2 min (three mice).

Criterion: pHAb dF/F of one ganglion-cell ROI per mouse, photobleaching corrected, averaged over three mice; 3.7% read (a) as the mean dF/F at 15 s after onset, (b) as the peak within 15 s; within tolerance (3.33 to 4.07%, rate 0.178 to 0.410 %/s) under one reading, and back within the pre-stimulus mean plus 2 SD by 120 s.

The deposit does not say which recordings are the three mice of Fig. 5B. It holds two 3 V, 100-pulse recordings of the ACh nanosensor: sub-2 (the 3 V recording of the AQuA mouse) and sub-6 after washout (the untreated recording of the vesamicol pair). Both are used, alone and averaged. Onset is frame 19 (10.45 s, Fig. 6A and 7A). The ROI is open: (i) the stained tissue, (ii) the whole frame, (iii) the tissue without the pixels that saturate at some frame, (iv) each 40 x 40 pixel block (about one cell) inside the tissue, as the distribution the hand-drawn ROI was drawn from. A further ROI subtracts the camera's dark level (data check) from the tissue mean. Photobleaching curve fit to (a) the frames before onset and from 120 s after it, (c) the frames before onset and from 180 s after it, as sub-2 is not back at 120 s (for sub-6 at 0.50 s there are too few frames after 180 s, and the whole trace is used), (b) the whole trace; baseline mean of pre-onset frames or the first frame; frame interval 0.50 s (the files) or 0.55 s (the paper). Rates: (a) a line from onset to the peak within 15 s; (b) the slope over k = 2 to 5 frames, counted from the last frame before the trace leaves baseline (|z| > 5 against frames 0 to 18), since the responses start 6 to 10 frames after frame 19. The k-frame slopes from frame 19 are printed too; they cover baseline frames and are not counted as a match.

ON = X.STIM_FRAME

def response(tr, dt, bl, base):
    n = len(tr)
    after = {"a": 120, "c": 180}.get(bl)
    rec = ON + int(round(after / dt)) if after else n
    idx = np.r_[0:ON, rec:n] if (after and rec < n - 5) else np.arange(n)
    corr, _ = X.bleach_correct(tr, idx)
    d = X.dff(corr, ON, base)
    f15 = ON + int(round(15 / dt))
    pre = d[:ON]
    z = (d - pre.mean()) / pre.std()
    dep = ON + int(np.argmax(np.abs(z[ON:]) > 5)) - 1     # last frame before the trace leaves baseline (|z| > 5)
    out = {"at15": d[f15], "peak15": d[ON + 1:f15 + 1].max(), "rate_peak": X.initial_rate(d, ON, dt, "peak", f15 + 1), "departure": dep}
    for k in (2, 3, 4, 5):
        out[f"rate_k{k}"] = X.initial_rate(d, ON, dt, f"k{k}")
        out[f"rate_dep_k{k}"] = X.initial_rate(d, dep, dt, f"k{k}")
    i120 = min(ON + int(round(120 / dt)), n - 1)
    out["d120"] = d[i120]
    out["thr120"] = pre.mean() + 2 * pre.std()
    return out, d

REC5B = {"sub-2 3V": "right", "sub-6 without drug": "single"}

readings with dF/F within tolerance: 0 of 144; with the rate to the peak or a rate from the departure within: 0; both: 0
dF/F at 15 s over all readings: 17.1 to 40.1%; peak within 15 s 17.6 to 40.1%; rate to the peak 1.54 to 3.33 %/s; rates over k frames from the departure -0.81 to 4.20 %/s
departure frames (last frame before |z| > 5): sub-2 [26, 27, 28], sub-6 [25, 26, 27, 29]
rates over k frames from frame 19 (stimulation onset), which cover baseline frames before the departure: -7.46 to 0.83 %/s; readings where one is within 0.178-0.410 %/s: 54 (not counted as a match)
sub-2 3V: dF/F at 120 s 9.4 to 16.4%; back within pre-stimulus mean + 2 SD in 0 of 48 readings
sub-6 without drug: dF/F at 120 s 0.6 to 12.2%; back within pre-stimulus mean + 2 SD in 14 of 48 readings
ROI tissue, mean of both: dF/F at 15 s 20.8 to 23.2%
ROI tissue_minus_dark, mean of both: dF/F at 15 s 21.9 to 24.4%

Per 40 x 40 block (dt 0.50 s, bleach a, mean baseline):

  sub-2 3V: 21 blocks; dF/F at 15 s 11.3 to 53.6% (median 25.9); rate to peak 0.65 to 4.32 %/s; blocks with dF/F within tolerance 0, with a rate within 0, both 0
  sub-6 without drug: 13 blocks; dF/F at 15 s 0.3 to 28.4% (median 17.6); rate to peak 0.03 to 2.82 %/s; blocks with dF/F within tolerance 1, with a rate within 1, both 1

Result: not reproduced. Under every reading the pHAb dF/F 15 s after onset is far above 3.7%: 17.1 to 40.1% (0 of 144 readings within 3.33 to 4.07%), 23.0 to 29.6% in sub-2 and 17.1 to 40.1% in sub-6 after washout. Subtracting the camera's dark level raises it slightly (mean of both, tissue: 20.8 to 23.2% without, 21.9 to 24.4% with). Single 40 x 40 pixel blocks, about one cell each, give 11.3 to 53.6% in sub-2 and 0.3 to 28.4% in sub-6; one block of sub-6 is within tolerance in both dF/F and rate. The rate to the peak is 1.54 to 3.33 %/s, and the rates over 2 to 5 frames from the frame where each trace leaves baseline (frames 25 to 29) are -0.81 to 4.20 %/s; none of the readings has a rate within 0.178 to 0.410 %/s by these measures. Rates over 2 to 5 frames from frame 19 fall within it in 54 readings, but those frames lie before the response, so they measure baseline and are not counted. At 120 s after onset sub-2 is still 9.4 to 16.4% above baseline under every bleaching fit, including the fit from 180 s; sub-6 is back within the pre-stimulus mean plus 2 SD in 14 of 48 readings, all with the fit from 120 s. The deposit does not say which recordings are the three mice of Fig. 5B; on the two 3 V recordings it holds, the response is about 5 to 10 times the paper's.

fig6-vesamicol¶

Vesamicol cuts the nanosensor response to 3 V stimulation; in the example the response with the drug is 17% of that after washout, and over four experiments the reduction averages 76.59 ± 11.34%, significant in each by a paired t test (P < 0.01).

Criterion: peak pHAb dF/F with vesamicol and after washout, same ROI and stimulation, normalised to the maximum; reduction is 1 minus the ratio, averaged over four experiments; tests (a) one paired t test over the four experiments' peaks, (b) a paired t test within each experiment over matched time points from onset to the end of the response. The deposit holds one experiment (sub-6), taken as the example of Fig. 6A-B. Peak: the maximum dF/F from onset (frame 19, Fig. 6A "Sti starts 10.45 s") to 120 s after it. End of the response for (b): 120 s after onset (the paper's "within 2 min"). ROI open: stained tissue, whole frame, the tissue without pixels that saturate at some frame, and the same 40 x 40 blocks in both files (the two files are one field; their shift is printed). Photobleaching and baseline readings as in fig5b. sub-6 has single frames that drop below their neighbours (counted below); a 3-frame median filter is shown as a variant. The frames of test (b) are not independent (each follows the last), so the test is also run on the means of non-overlapping 10 s bins, as a variant.

from skimage.registration import phase_cross_correlation
print("shift between the mean images of the two sub-6 files:", phase_cross_correlation(V["sub-6 with drug"]["single"]["mean_img"], V["sub-6 without drug"]["single"]["mean_img"])[0])
for k in ("sub-6 with drug", "sub-6 without drug"):
    tr = V[k]["single"]["tissue"]
    dev = tr - ndi.median_filter(tr, 5)
    print(f"{k}: frames more than 5 SD below their 5-frame median: {int((dev < -5 * np.std(dev)).sum())} of {len(tr)}")

def peak_and_trace(tr, dt, bl, base, med=False):
    if med:
        tr = ndi.median_filter(tr, 3)
    n = len(tr); rec = ON + int(round(120 / dt))
    idx = np.r_[0:ON, rec:n] if (bl == "a" and rec < n - 5) else np.arange(n)
    corr, _ = X.bleach_correct(tr, idx)
    d = X.dff(corr, ON, base)
    end = min(rec, n - 1)
    return d[ON:end + 1].max(), d[ON:end + 1]

rows = []
for dt in (X.FRAME_S_FILE, X.FRAME_S_PAPER):
    for bl in ("a", "b"):
        for base in ("mean", "first"):
            for roi in ("tissue", "full", "tissue_unsat"):
                for med in (False, True):
                    pw, dw = peak_and_trace(V["sub-6 with drug"]["single"][roi], dt, bl, base, med)
                    po, do = peak_and_trace(V["sub-6 without drug"]["single"][roi], dt, bl, base, med)
                    m = min(len(dw), len(do))
                    tt = stats.ttest_rel(dw[:m], do[:m])
                    nb_ = int(round(10 / dt)); nbins = m // nb_   # variant: means of non-overlapping 10 s bins, fewer and less dependent samples
                    tb = stats.ttest_rel(dw[:nbins * nb_].reshape(nbins, nb_).mean(1), do[:nbins * nb_].reshape(nbins, nb_).mean(1))
                    rows.append({"dt": dt, "bleach": bl, "baseline": base, "roi": roi, "median3": med, "peak_with": round(pw, 2), "peak_without": round(po, 2),
                                 "ratio_%": round(100 * pw / po, 1), "reduction_%": round(100 * (1 - pw / po), 1), "paired_t": round(tt.statistic, 2), "p": tt.pvalue, "n_frames": m,
                                 "t_10s_bins": round(tb.statistic, 2), "p_10s_bins": tb.pvalue, "n_bins": nbins})
R6 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
R6["ratio_ok"] = (R6["ratio_%"] - 17).abs() <= 1.7
R6["reduction_ok"] = (R6["reduction_%"] - 76.59).abs() <= 11.34
print(R6.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nratio within 15.3-18.7%: {int(R6.ratio_ok.sum())} of {len(R6)}; reduction within 65.25-87.93%: {int(R6.reduction_ok.sum())}; "
      f"ratio range {R6['ratio_%'].min():.1f} to {R6['ratio_%'].max():.1f}%; largest p of the within-experiment t test {R6.p.max():.2g}")
print(f"paired t over the means of 10 s bins ({R6.n_bins.min()} to {R6.n_bins.max()} bins): p {R6.p_10s_bins.min():.2g} to {R6.p_10s_bins.max():.2g}; "
      f"below 0.01 in {int((R6.p_10s_bins < 0.01).sum())} of {len(R6)} readings")

ow = V["sub-6 with drug"]["single"]["origins"]; oo = V["sub-6 without drug"]["single"]["origins"]

Result: partially reproduced. The deposit holds one of the four experiments. In it vesamicol cuts the response: over 48 readings the peak with the drug is 11.3 to 29.9% of the peak after washout, a reduction of 70.1 to 88.7%, within the paper's 76.59 ± 11.34% in 44 readings. The paired t test over matched frames of the two traces gives p of 4.9e-11 or smaller in every reading, but its frames are not independent; over the means of twelve 10 s bins it gives p of 2.2e-06 to 0.14, below 0.01 in 37 of 48 readings; under the first reading (0.50 s, fit a, mean baseline, tissue) it is 0.0103, not below 0.01. The example's 17% is matched in 24 of 48 readings and depends on the ROI: the stained tissue gives 17.5 to 22.3% with the mean baseline and 28.0 to 29.9% with the first frame, the whole frame 13.0 to 17.0%, and the tissue without saturating pixels 11.3 to 17.6%. 69% of the tissue pixels of the washout recording saturate at some frame (data check), which clips its peak and raises the ratio when they are kept. Cell-sized blocks give ratios of 13.3 to 437.3% (median 36.8%), none within 15.3 to 18.7%, as blocks with little response after washout give large ratios. The mean over four experiments and the paired test over them (reading a) cannot be computed. Partially reproduced: the suppression holds in the one deposited experiment, three of four are not deposited, and the example ratio depends on the ROI.

figs16-af647-stable¶

The AF647 channel recorded with the pHAb signal of Figure 7 shows no visible fluorescence increase during stimulation, so the internal standard does not respond.

Criterion: whole-SMG mean AF647 intensity, photobleaching corrected, over the 8 V recording; reproduced when its largest rise after stimulation onset is below the largest rise of the pHAb channel by at least a factor of five and within the pre-stimulus noise (mean plus 3 SD). The 8 V recording is sub-3 (Methods: one mouse stimulated at 3 and 8 V for Fig. 7). The left half is taken as AF647 and the right as pHAb (data check; an assumption). The whole SMG is read as (i) the tissue mask of each channel, (ii) the whole half-frame, (iii) the pHAb tissue mask applied to the AF647 half. Photobleaching curve fit to (a) the frames before onset and from 120 s after it, (b) the whole trace. Rises are dF/F against the pre-onset mean. The drop of both channels right after stimulation is shown, with the AF647 rise measured from its lowest point as a variant.

Result: reproduced, resting on the channel assignment. Over the 8 V recording the AF647 channel's largest rise after onset is 0.4 to 3.7%, within its pre-stimulus mean plus 3 SD (1.9 to 4.1%) under all six readings, while the pHAb channel rises by 46.9 to 54.0%, 14 to 135 times more. The AF647 channel drops by 13 to 15% after stimulation, as the pHAb channel does at first (data check), and rises by 11.1 to 16.5% from that minimum. After the minimum it passes its pre-stimulus mean in 3 of 6 readings (by 1.35 to 2.77%, all with the bleaching curve fit outside the response), and its pre-stimulus mean plus 3 SD in none. The files do not label the channels; the left half is taken as AF647 because it does not rise, so the test shows that one channel stays flat while the other rises, which is what the claim needs if the assignment is right.

fig7-rostral-caudal¶

At 8 V, AQuA shows the nanosensor signal spreading from rostral to caudal across the SMG. The rostral-most region rises at 13.20 s (2.75 s after stimulation onset) and peaks at 22.0 s; the signal reaches caudal regions by 13.75 and 15.40 s and lateral at 15.95 s; the most caudal region peaks at 44.55 s.

Criterion: AQuA on the 8 V recording of Figure 7 (stimulation 10.45 to 20.35 s), the whole SMG; reproduced when the event onsets are ordered rostral before caudal before lateral and the times are within tolerance (onsets within 0.55 s, the rostral peak within 0.55 s, the caudal peak within 4.455 s); partially reproduced when the order holds but the times do not.

AQuA is not run, and a substitute is. AQuA (Wang et al. 2019, the paper's ref. 32) is MATLAB software; it cannot be installed in the entry's locked Python environment, and the paper names its parameters (intensity threshold scaling factor, Gaussian smoothing, temporal cut threshold, super-event grouping; Methods, AQuA Analysis) without values. In its place each 16 x 16 pixel block of the pHAb tissue mask gets an onset and a peak frame (X.block_onsets: photobleaching-corrected dF/F; onset the first frame from frame 19 that begins 3 frames above the block's pre-onset mean + 3 SD; peak the largest 3-frame mean). The bleaching curve is fit to the frames before onset and from 120 s after it (a); variants fit it from 180 s after onset (c) or to the whole trace (b), and use blocks of 32 pixels and thresholds of 2 and 5 SD. This is an assumption: it measures where and when the signal rises, as AQuA's events do, but it is not AQuA, and AQuA's events and their times may differ from block onsets.

Regions and axis. The anatomical axis is read from Figure 7B, as the criterion says: rostral up (the stimulating electrode), caudal down, lateral to the left. The files carry no orientation; the frame is taken as shown in Figure 7A. (While preparing, outside this notebook, the panels of Fig. 7A were compared with the frames of sub-3: they show the right half of the frame, not flipped. That comparison is not run here, as the entry reads no figures.) The orientation decides the direction: the cell below runs the frame turned each way. That the deposited frames are oriented as Figure 7A shows them, with rostral up, is an assumption: the files are the camera's frames, the paper shows no sign of a flip, and the criterion reads the axis from Figure 7B. The paper's four AQuA areas cannot be located from the text, so four regions are drawn from the axis: the rostral, middle and caudal thirds of the tissue's extent along the rows (region 1, rostral-most; regions 2 and 3, the caudal regions the text reaches "by 13.75 and 15.40 s"; "most caudal" is the caudal third), and the lateral region 4, the blocks of the lower two thirds in the quarter of columns furthest to the left. A region's onset is the median onset of its blocks (the earliest is also printed), and its peak the median peak frame. Times are frame x 0.55 s, the paper's clock, on which stimulation starts at 10.45 s (frame 19); the files' 0.50 s clock is printed too. The 8 V recording is sub-3.

In [20]:
def regions(a, mask):
    rows_ = np.flatnonzero(mask.any(1)); top, bot = rows_.min(), rows_.max()
    rc = (a[:, 0] - top) / (bot - top)
    lower = a[rc >= 1 / 3]
    left_cut = np.percentile(lower[:, 1], 25)
    return {"1 rostral third": a[rc < 1 / 3], "2 middle third": a[(rc >= 1 / 3) & (rc < 2 / 3)], "3 caudal third": a[rc >= 2 / 3],
            "4 lateral (left quarter of lower 2/3)": lower[lower[:, 1] <= left_cut]}

def flipped(a, mask, rows_flip, cols_flip):
    a = a.copy()
    r_, c_ = np.flatnonzero(mask.any(1)), np.flatnonzero(mask.any(0))
    if rows_flip:
        a[:, 0] = r_.min() + r_.max() - a[:, 0]
    if cols_flip:
        a[:, 1] = c_.min() + c_.max() - a[:, 1]
    return a

ORIENT = (((False, False), "as deposited (rostral up, lateral left)"), ((True, False), "flipped top to bottom"),
          ((False, True), "flipped left to right"), ((True, True), "turned 180 degrees"))

def region_table(key, flip=(False, False)):
    mask = V[key]["right"]["mask"]
    out = []
    for (k_, size, k, fit), a in MAPS.items():
        if k_ != key:
            continue
        a = flipped(a[a[:, 2] >= 0], mask, *flip)
        rg = regions(a, mask)
        row = {"block px": size, "k SD": k, "bleach fit": fit, "blocks with onset": len(a),
               "rho(onset, row)": round(stats.spearmanr(a[:, 0], a[:, 2])[0], 2), "p(rho row)": stats.spearmanr(a[:, 0], a[:, 2])[1],
               "rho(onset, column)": round(stats.spearmanr(a[:, 1], a[:, 2])[0], 2)}
        for name, r in rg.items():
            n_ = name.split()[0]
            row[f"R{n_} n"] = len(r)
            row[f"R{n_} onset"] = float(np.median(r[:, 2])); row[f"R{n_} first"] = float(r[:, 2].min())
            row[f"R{n_} peak"] = float(np.median(r[:, 3])); row[f"R{n_} amp %"] = round(float(np.median(r[:, 4])), 1)
        row["order 1<2,3<4"] = bool(row["R1 onset"] < min(row["R2 onset"], row["R3 onset"]) and max(row["R2 onset"], row["R3 onset"]) < row["R4 onset"])
        row["order 1<2<=3<4"] = bool(row["R1 onset"] < row["R2 onset"] <= row["R3 onset"] < row["R4 onset"])
        out.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

The files carry no orientation. The order under each way the frame could be turned (regions redrawn on the turned frame):

  as deposited (rostral up, lateral left): rostral < caudal regions < lateral in 18 of 18 variants; rostral region first in 18
  flipped top to bottom: rostral < caudal regions < lateral in 0 of 18 variants; rostral region first in 0
  flipped left to right: rostral < caudal regions < lateral in 0 of 18 variants; rostral region first in 18
  turned 180 degrees: rostral < caudal regions < lateral in 0 of 18 variants; rostral region first in 0

sub-3 8V maps: 157 blocks, 0 without an onset; onset frames 27 to 45, peak frames 51 to 129; rostral is up
sub-2 3V maps: 154 blocks, 0 without an onset; onset frames 25 to 46, peak frames 43 to 77; rostral is up

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the substitute for AQuA and on the orientation. In sub-3 the signal starts rostrally and spreads caudally and then laterally: in all 18 variants the median onset of the rostral third precedes those of the middle and caudal thirds, which precede the lateral region (for 16 px blocks, 3 SD, fit a: frames 30, 34, 37 and 42), and block onset rises with the rostro-caudal position (Spearman rho 0.62 to 0.68, p 0.00011 or less) and falls with the column (rho -0.63 to -0.44, later to the left, the lateral side). The times do not match: on the paper's clock the region onsets are 15.95 to 16.50 s (rostral), 17.60 to 19.25 s, 19.80 to 20.90 s and 22.00 to 23.65 s (lateral), against 13.20, 13.75, 15.40 and 15.95 s; the rostral peak is 30.25 to 34.10 s against 22.0 s and the caudal peak 35.75 to 36.30 s against 44.55 s; none of the 36 variant-clock pairs has any of the six times within tolerance. Part of the onset delay may come from the drop of both channels in the first frames after stimulation (data check), which a threshold on dF/F has to clear, and AQuA's events need not match blocks. The direction rests on the orientation: with the frame flipped top to bottom, or turned 180 degrees, the order holds in 0 of 18 variants, and flipped left to right also in 0 of 18 (the rostral region still starts first in all 18, but the lateral region no longer comes last). The frame is taken as deposited, rostral up, an assumption (see above). Partially reproduced, as the criterion says when the order holds but the times do not, on the frame as deposited.

fig7-peak-timing¶

All evoked nanosensor responses in Figure 7A climb to their peak around 10 to 15 s after stimulation onset, as in Figure 5B to E.

Criterion: for the AQuA events of Figure 7A, the time to each event's peak, from (i) stimulation onset (10.45 s) or (ii) the event's onset; reproduced when, under one reading, all four numbered events peak within 9 to 16.5 s; partially reproduced when all but the most caudal do. As for fig7-rostral-caudal, the four regions and the block onsets and peaks stand in for AQuA's events (an assumption), on sub-3. The per-block times are shown too.

i from stimulation onset: all four within 9-16.5 s in 0 of 36 variants; all but the caudal region in 0; times 18.0 to 26.4 s
ii from region onset: all four within 9-16.5 s in 30 of 36 variants; all but the caudal region in 30; times 11.8 to 18.1 s
the paper's own times (claim fig7-rostral-caudal): reading (i) rostral 11.55 s, most caudal 34.10 s; reading (ii) rostral 8.80 s, most caudal 29.15 s (9-16.5 s to pass)
per block (16 px, 3 SD, bleach a, 0.55 s), time to peak from stimulation onset: 17.6 to 60.5 s, median 23.7; within 9-16.5 s: 0 of 157
per block (16 px, 3 SD, bleach a, 0.55 s), time to peak from block onset: 9.4 to 55.6 s, median 13.8; within 9-16.5 s: 126 of 157

Result: reproduced under reading (ii), resting on the substitute for AQuA and on the orientation; asked of a reader. Counted from each region's onset (reading ii), the four regions of sub-3 reach their peak in 11.8 to 18.1 s; all four are within 9 to 16.5 s in 30 of 36 variants, every variant with the bleaching curve fit outside the response (a and c) on both clocks, and at the 0.50 s clock with the whole-trace fit. For the main variant (16 px blocks, 3 SD, fit a, paper's clock) the times are 14.30, 14.85, 15.40 and 13.48 s, and 126 of the 157 blocks peak 9 to 16.5 s after their own onset (median 13.8 s). Counted from stimulation onset (reading i), no variant fits: the regions peak 18.0 to 26.4 s after it, and no block peaks within 16.5 s of it. The pass is weak. It rests on the region onsets, which come 2.75 to 3.3 s after the paper's for the rostral region (none of the six times of fig7-rostral-caudal matches); both the onsets and the peaks are late, and their difference falls in the window. And reading (ii) does not fit the paper's own times: from Figure 7B and the text, the rostral region peaks 8.80 s after its onset and the most caudal 29.15 s after its own, both outside 9 to 16.5 s, while reading (i) gives 11.55 s for the rostral region. The claims file flags the paper's contradiction only for the most caudal region; whether reading (ii) should stand is now asked of a reader (questions/xia-2021.yaml). The outcome follows the claims file as written, which counts a pass under either reading: reproduced under reading (ii).

figs12-3v-propagation¶

At 3 V, in three independent experiments, AQuA shows the same rostral-to-caudal direction of propagation, with lower amplitude than at 8 V.

Criterion: AQuA as in fig7-rostral-caudal on the 3 V recordings of three mice (one also used at 8 V, two at 3 V only); reproduced when in each the earliest event lies rostral of the later ones, and in the mouse stimulated at both voltages the peak dF/F at 3 V is below that at 8 V; partially reproduced when two of three show the order. Only the mouse stimulated at both voltages is deposited: sub-2 (3 V) and sub-3 (8 V) are one ganglion (data check). The two mice stimulated at 3 V only are not. The block maps stand in for AQuA, as above (an assumption). Order: the rostral region's onset precedes those of the other regions, and the earliest block lies in the rostral third. Amplitude: the peak of the photobleaching-corrected tissue dF/F after onset, at 3 V and 8 V.

3 V below 8 V in 6 of 6 readings; block-median amplitude by region at 3 V and 8 V (16 px, 3 SD, bleach a): R1 43.6 vs 69.9; R2 28.1 vs 53.9; R3 21.5 vs 39.5; R4 21.1 vs 38.0

Result: blocked, data missing (one deposited mouse of three). The results in that one mouse rest on the substitute for AQuA and on the orientation. In the mouse stimulated at both voltages the 3 V response is lower than the 8 V one in all 6 readings (tissue peak 27.1 to 29.0% against 46.9 to 54.0%), and in each of the four regions (block medians 21.1 to 43.6% against 38.0 to 69.9%). At 3 V the rostral region's onset precedes the other three in 12 of 18 variants, all those with the bleaching curve fit outside the response (a and c); with the curve fit to the whole trace (b), which takes in part of a response still 9 to 16% above baseline at 120 s (fig5b-in-vivo-response), it does not. Every earliest block lies in the rostral third in 11 of 18 variants, and block onset rises with the rostro-caudal position in the fits outside the response (rho 0.42 to 0.74). With the frame flipped top to bottom or turned 180 degrees, the rostral region starts first in 0 of 18 variants, so the direction rests on the orientation, as for fig7-rostral-caudal. The two mice stimulated at 3 V only are not deposited. The criterion's partial outcome needs the order in two of three mice, which one mouse cannot give, and its full outcome needs all three, so the criterion cannot be applied. The outcome verified in round 1 was partially reproduced; the round-2 verifier found that the threshold cannot be reached, and the round-3 verifier agreed with the change to blocked, for missing data, with the results in this one mouse reported as above. If the two missing mice are deposited, rostral is to be read from the electrode side, as the criterion says, not from the orientation assumed here.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The ROIs of Figs. 5 and 6 are drawn by hand in the paper and not given; whole-tissue, whole-frame, saturation-free and cell-sized block ROIs are used instead. The stimulation onset is taken from Fig. 6A and 7A (10.45 s, frame 19) for every in vivo recording, as the files do not record it; the ACh addition in the ex vivo recordings is taken as the largest one-frame rise. The frame interval is run at the paper's 0.55 s and at the 0.50 s the files record. Fig. 4B is fit on one mouse of three and 8 concentrations; Fig. 5B on two 3 V recordings whose identity with the paper's three mice is not known; Fig. 6 on one experiment of four. Colocalisation is judged by eye with a threshold rule from the claims file, a background and masks chosen here. AQuA (MATLAB, with parameters the paper does not give) was not run; for Fig. 7 and S12 the onset and peak of 16 x 16 pixel blocks, grouped into rostral, middle, caudal and lateral regions, stand in for its events, on the frame as deposited (rostral up), an assumption on which the direction of propagation rests. The HPLC flow rate is not given, so the retention volumes are not tested; the end of the second peak is taken where its descent ends.

What was found about the datasets. SPARC:108 holds a part of the paper's data: one of three calibration mice, one of four vesamicol experiments, the 3 V and 8 V recordings of the AQuA mouse (as two subjects, sub-2 and sub-3, of one ganglion), one 10 V recording with a single stimulation, and none of the control nanosensor, pH, 5 V, pulse-number, repeated-stimulation, AFM, stability, two-photon or fiber data. The primary manifest.xlsx names 40 of its 50 files under names that are not in the dataset, seven of the eight calibration files lack an extension, and the sheet describes the calibration recordings as electrical stimulation. The recordings carry no channel labels, no spatial scale, no stimulation or addition times, and, for the files resaved in ImageJ, no frame times; the files that keep frame times show 0.50 s, where the paper uses 0.55 s. Many tissue pixels saturate in the sub-6 recordings (69% at some frame after washout). In SPARC:75 the high-magnification BTX stack has 50 empty planes out of 62. SPARC:108 names the bioRxiv preprint, not the PNAS paper, as its originating article; SPARC:75 names none.
